title: Mutating Data
description: Learn how to mutate data using Server Functions and Server Actions in Next.js.
related:
  title: API Reference
  description: Learn more about the features mentioned in this page by reading the API Reference.
  links:
    - app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath

    - app/api-reference/functions/redirect
---

You can mutate data in Next.js using [React Server Functions](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-functions). This page will go through how you can [create](#creating-server-functions) and [invoke](#invoking-server-functions) Server Functions.

## What are Server Functions?

A **Server Function** is an asynchronous function that runs on the server. You can call them from the client through a network request, which is why they must be asynchronous.

In an `action` or mutation context, they are also called **Server Actions**.

title: Mutating Data
description: Learn how to mutate data using Server Functions and Server Actions in Next.js.

  title: API Reference
  description: Learn more about the features mentioned in this page by reading the API Reference.

You can mutate data in Next.js using [React Server Functions](https://react.dev/reference/rsc/server-functions). This page will go through how you can [create](#creating-server-functions) and [invoke](#invoking-server-functions) Server Functions.

## What are Server Functions?

A **Server Function** is an asynchronous function that runs on the server. You can call them from the client through a network request, which is why they must be asynchronous.

In an `action` or mutation context, they are also called **Server Actions**.

> This page covers caching with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide.

Caching is a technique for storing the result of data fetching and other computations so that future requests for the same data can be served faster, without doing the work again.

## Enabling Cache Components

You can enable Cache Components by adding the [`cacheComponents`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) option to your Next config file:

00002| title: Revalidating
00003| description: Learn how to revalidate cached data using time-based and on-demand strategies.
00004| related:
00005|   title: API Reference
00006|   description: Learn more about the APIs mentioned on this page.
00007|   links:
00008|     - app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife

00011|     - app/api-reference/functions/updateTag

00013| ---
00014| 
00015| > This page covers revalidation with [Cache Components](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents), enabled by setting [`cacheComponents: true`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheComponents) in your `next.config.ts` file. If you're not using Cache Components, see the [Caching and Revalidating (Previous Model)](/docs/app/guides/caching-without-cache-components) guide.
00016| 
00017| Revalidation is the process of updating cached data. It lets you keep serving fast, cached responses while ensuring content stays fresh. There are two strategies:
00018| 
00019| - **Time-based revalidation**: Automatically refresh cached data after a set duration using [`cacheLife`](#cachelife).
00020| - **On-demand revalidation**: Manually invalidate cached data after a mutation using [`revalidateTag`](#revalidatetag), [`updateTag`](#updatetag), or [`revalidatePath`](#revalidatepath).
00021| 
00022| ## `cacheLife`
00023| 
00024| [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) controls how long cached data remains valid. Use it inside a [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) scope to set the cache lifetime.
00025| 
00026| ```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" highlight={1,4,5}
00027| import { cacheLife } from 'next/cache'
00028| 
00029| export async function getProducts() {
00030|   'use cache'
00031|   cacheLife('hours')
00032|   return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
00033| }
00034| ```
00035| 
00036| `cacheLife` accepts a profile name or a custom configuration object:
00037| 
00038| | Profile   | `stale` | `revalidate` | `expire` |
00039| | --------- | ------- | ------------ | -------- |
00040| | `default` | 5m      | 15m          | never    |
00041| | `seconds` | 30s     | 1s           | 60s      |
00042| | `minutes` | 5m      | 1m           | 1h       |
00043| | `hours`   | 5m      | 1h           | 1d       |
00044| | `days`    | 5m      | 1d           | 1w       |
00045| | `weeks`   | 5m      | 1w           | 30d      |
00046| | `max`     | 5m      | 30d          | 1y       |
00047| 
00048| For fine-grained control, pass an object:
00049| 
00050| ```tsx highlight={2-6}
00051| 'use cache'
00052| cacheLife({
00053|   stale: 3600, // 1 hour until considered stale
00054|   revalidate: 7200, // 2 hours until revalidated
00055|   expire: 86400, // 1 day until expired
00056| })
00057| ```
00058| 
00059| > **Good to know:** A cache is considered "short-lived" when it uses the `seconds` profile, `revalidate: 0`, or `expire` under 5 minutes. Short-lived caches are automatically excluded from prerenders and become dynamic holes instead. See [Prerendering behavior](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife#prerendering-behavior) for details.
00060| 
00061| See the [`cacheLife` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) for all profiles and custom configuration options.
00062| 
00063| ## `cacheTag`
00064| 
00065| [`cacheTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) lets you tag cached data so it can be invalidated on-demand. Use it inside a [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) scope:
00066| 
00067| ```tsx filename="app/lib/data.ts" switcher
00068| import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
00069| 
00070| export async function getProducts() {
00071|   'use cache'
00072|   cacheTag('products')
00073|   return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
00074| }
00075| ```
00076| 
00077| ```jsx filename="app/lib/data.js" switcher
00078| import { cacheTag } from 'next/cache'
00079| 
00080| export async function getProducts() {
00081|   'use cache'
00082|   cacheTag('products')
00083|   return db.query('SELECT * FROM products')
00084| }
00085| ```
00086| 
00087| Once tagged, invalidate the cache using [`revalidateTag`](#revalidatetag) or [`updateTag`](#updatetag).
00088| 
00089| See the [`cacheTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) to learn more.
00090| 
00091| ## `revalidateTag`
00092| 
00093| `revalidateTag` invalidates cache entries by tag using stale-while-revalidate semantics — stale content is served immediately while fresh content loads in the background. This is ideal for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, like blog posts or product catalogs.
00094| 
00095| ```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,5} switcher
00096| import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
00097| 
00098| export async function updateUser(id: string) {
00099|   // Mutate data
00100|   revalidateTag('user', 'max') // Recommended: stale-while-revalidate
00101| }
00102| ```
00103| 
00104| ```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,5} switcher
00105| import { revalidateTag } from 'next/cache'
00106| 
00107| export async function updateUser(id) {
00108|   // Mutate data
00109|   revalidateTag('user', 'max') // Recommended: stale-while-revalidate
00110| }
00111| ```
00112| 
00113| You can reuse the same tag in multiple functions to revalidate them all at once. Call `revalidateTag` in a [Server Action](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data) or [Route Handler](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route).
00114| 
00115| > **Good to know:** The second argument sets how long stale content can be served while fresh content generates in the background. Once it expires, subsequent requests block until fresh content is ready. Using `'max'` gives the longest stale window.
00116| 
00117| See the [`revalidateTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) to learn more.
00118| 
00119| ## `updateTag`
00120| 
00121| `updateTag` immediately expires cached data for read-your-own-writes scenarios — the user sees their change right away instead of stale content. Unlike `revalidateTag`, it can only be used in [Server Actions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data).
00122| 
00123| ```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,12} switcher
00124| import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
00125| import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
00126| 
00127| export async function createPost(formData: FormData) {
00128|   const post = await db.post.create({
00129|     data: {
00130|       title: formData.get('title'),
00131|       content: formData.get('content'),
00132|     },
00133|   })
00134| 
00135|   updateTag('posts')
00136|   redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
00137| }
00138| ```
00139| 
00140| ```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,12} switcher
00141| import { updateTag } from 'next/cache'
00142| import { redirect } from 'next/navigation'
00143| 
00144| export async function createPost(formData) {
00145|   const post = await db.post.create({
00146|     data: {
00147|       title: formData.get('title'),
00148|       content: formData.get('content'),
00149|     },
00150|   })
00151| 
00152|   updateTag('posts')
00153|   redirect(`/posts/${post.id}`)
00154| }
00155| ```
00156| 
00157| |              | `updateTag`                                   | `revalidateTag`                      |
00158| | ------------ | --------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------ |
00159| | **Where**    | Server Actions only                           | Server Actions and Route Handlers    |
00160| | **Behavior** | Immediately expires cache                     | Stale-while-revalidate               |
00161| | **Use case** | Read-your-own-writes (user sees their change) | Background refresh (slight delay OK) |
00162| 
00163| See the [`updateTag` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag) to learn more.
00164| 
00165| ## `revalidatePath`
00166| 
00167| `revalidatePath` invalidates all cached data for a specific route path. Use it when you want to revalidate a route without knowing which tags are associated with it.
00168| 
00169| ```tsx filename="app/lib/actions.ts" highlight={1,5} switcher
00170| import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'
00171| 
00172| export async function updateUser(id: string) {
00173|   // Mutate data
00174|   revalidatePath('/profile')
00175| }
00176| ```
00177| 
00178| ```jsx filename="app/lib/actions.js" highlight={1,5} switcher
00179| import { revalidatePath } from 'next/cache'
00180| 
00181| export async function updateUser(id) {
00182|   // Mutate data
00183|   revalidatePath('/profile')
00184| }
00185| ```
00186| 
00187| > **Good to know**: Prefer tag-based revalidation (`revalidateTag`/`updateTag`) over path-based when possible — it's more precise and avoids over-invalidating.
00188| 
00189| See the [`revalidatePath` API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath) to learn more.
00190| 
00191| ## What should I cache?
00192| 
00193| Cache data that doesn't depend on [runtime data](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#working-with-runtime-apis) and that you're OK serving from cache for a period of time. Use `use cache` with `cacheLife` to describe that behavior.
00194| 
00195| For content management systems with update mechanisms, use tags with longer cache durations and rely on `revalidateTag` to refresh content when it actually changes, rather than expiring the cache preemptively.
00196| 
00197| > **Good to know:** In serverless environments, in-memory cache entries may not persist across revalidations. See [runtime caching considerations](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache#runtime-caching-considerations) for details.
00198|

00002| title: How revalidation works in Next.js
00003| nav_title: How Revalidation Works
00004| description: A deep dive into how Next.js revalidates cached content, including the tag system, cache consistency, and multi-instance coordination.
00005| related:
00006|   description: Related guides and references.
00007|   links:
00008|     - app/getting-started/caching
00009|     - app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration
00010|     - app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers
00011|     - app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag
00012| ---
00013| 
00014| The [Caching](/docs/app/getting-started/caching) page covers how to use `use cache`, `cacheTag`, and `cacheLife`. This page explains **how revalidation works internally**, for platform engineers and advanced users who need to understand the system to implement [custom cache handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers) or debug revalidation behavior.
00015| 
00016| ## The Revalidation Model
00017| 
00018| Most routes in Next.js can be revalidated on demand. This includes App Router routes and Pages Router routes that produce ISR/prerender cache entries. Pages Router routes that are automatically statically optimized (pure static output) are not revalidated on demand. The ability to update cached content without redeploying is a core part of Next.js's [rendering model](/docs/app/guides/rendering-philosophy).
00019| 
00020| There are two types of revalidation:
00021| 
00022| - **Time-based revalidation** uses a stale-while-revalidate pattern. The cached content is served immediately, and a background regeneration is triggered when the content's age exceeds the [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheLife) or `revalidate` duration. The stale content continues to be served until the fresh content is ready.
00023| - **On-demand revalidation** explicitly invalidates cached content by calling [`revalidateTag()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) or [`revalidatePath()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath). The next request to that content triggers a fresh render.
00024| 
00025| > **Good to know:** Pages Router on-demand ISR APIs (for example `res.revalidate()` and the `x-prerender-revalidate` flow) are still supported and use the server cache handler (`cacheHandler`, singular). The `cacheHandlers` option (plural) is for `'use cache'` directives.
00026| 
00027| ## What Gets Revalidated
00028| 
00029| When a route is revalidated, Next.js regenerates **both** the HTML response and the RSC payload (React Server Components payload) from the same React component tree. Both artifacts are stored together in the same cache entry.
00030| 
00031| This consistency matters because the RSC payload is used for client-side navigations. Browser navigations and client-side navigations should hold the same content.
00032| 
00033| ### What happens if they get out of sync
00034| 
00035| If a platform's cache serves HTML from one render and an RSC payload from a different render, users may see stale or mismatched content during client-side navigation. The primary mitigation is to cache HTML and RSC responses together with the same TTL and invalidation policy, and to respect the [`Vary` header](/docs/app/guides/cdn-caching) that Next.js sets. See [CDN Caching](/docs/app/guides/cdn-caching) for details.
00036| 
00037| A separate but related problem is **cross-deployment skew**: during rolling deployments, a client built with deploy A may receive responses from a server running deploy B. [`deploymentId`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/deploymentId) mitigates this: when the client detects a different deployment ID from the server, it triggers a hard navigation to fetch consistent content.
00038| 
00039| ## Tag System Architecture
00040| 
00041| Next.js uses a tag-based system to track which cached content needs to be invalidated. There are two types of tags:
00042| 
00043| ### Explicit tags
00044| 
00045| Explicit tags are set by the developer using [`cacheTag()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) inside a `use cache` function, or via `next: { tags: [...] }` on a `fetch` call. When [`revalidateTag('my-tag', 'max')`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) is called, all cache entries with that tag are invalidated.
00046| 
00047| ### Soft tags
00048| 
00049| Soft tags are automatically generated by Next.js based on the route path, prefixed with `_N_T_`. For example, the route `/blog/hello` generates soft tags like `_N_T_/layout`, `_N_T_/blog/layout`, `_N_T_/blog/hello/layout`, and `_N_T_/blog/hello`. Each segment in the path gets a layout tag, plus the leaf route itself.
00050| 
00051| Soft tags enable [`revalidatePath()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath) to work through the same tag-based system. When `revalidatePath('/blog/hello')` is called, it invalidates cache entries associated with that path's leaf route tag and its ancestor layout soft tags (for example `_N_T_/layout`, `_N_T_/blog/layout`, `_N_T_/blog/hello/layout`, and `_N_T_/blog/hello`).
00052| 
00053| In the [cache handler API](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers), soft tags are passed to the `get()` method as the `softTags` parameter. Your handler should check whether any soft tag has been invalidated after the cache entry's timestamp. The `getExpiration()` method returns the most recent revalidation timestamp across all provided tags, or `0` if none have been revalidated. It can also return `Infinity` to signal that the soft tags should instead be passed to `get()` and checked for expiration there. Your handler should treat an entry as stale if the returned timestamp is newer than the entry's own timestamp. See the [cache handler API reference](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers#getexpiration) for the full semantics.
00054| 
00055| ## Multi-Instance Considerations
00056| 
00057| When running multiple Next.js instances behind a load balancer, revalidation events are local by default. Calling `revalidateTag()` on instance A only invalidates the cache on that instance. Other instances continue serving the stale content until they learn about the invalidation.
00058| 
00059| The cache handler API provides two hooks for distributed coordination:
00060| 
00061| - **`updateTags()`** is called when `revalidateTag()` is invoked. Your handler should write the invalidation event to shared storage (for example, Redis or a database) so other instances can discover it.
00062| - **`refreshTags()`** is called periodically, but always before starting a new request. Your handler should check shared storage for recent invalidation events and update its local tag state accordingly.
00063| 
00064| For implementation details and a Redis example, see [Custom Cache Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers).
00065| 
00066| ## Implementation Patterns for Platforms
00067| 
00068| ### Single instance
00069| 
00070| The default file-system cache handles consistency automatically. Cache writes are atomic on the local filesystem, and tag state is maintained in memory. No additional configuration is needed.
00071| 
00072| ### Multi-instance with shared cache
00073| 
00074| Without coordination, each instance independently serves content and handles revalidation using only its local cache. Different users may see different content depending on which instance serves their request, and on-demand revalidation only takes effect on the instance that received the call.
00075| 
00076| To reduce this window and ensure revalidation propagates across instances:
00077| 
00078| 1. Store tag invalidation timestamps in a shared service (Redis, DynamoDB, or a simple HTTP API).
00079| 2. Implement `updateTags()` to write to the shared service.
00080| 3. Implement `refreshTags()` to read from the shared service. Your handler must catch errors in `refreshTags()`: if it throws, the exception propagates as a request failure. Catching the error allows requests to continue with the last known local tag state, serving potentially stale content until connectivity is restored.
00081| 4. Store cache entries (HTML + RSC payload) in shared storage. Atomic writes reduce the mismatch window further but are not required for correctness.
00082| 
00083| ### CDN integration
00084| 
00085| If a CDN caches Next.js responses, it should respect the `Vary` header and the `Cache-Control` directives that Next.js sets. Do not cache HTML and RSC payload responses separately with different TTLs. See [CDN Caching](/docs/app/guides/cdn-caching) for details.
00086| 
00087| ## Graceful Degradation
00088| 
00089| The revalidation system prioritizes availability over strict consistency. Content is always served, even when infrastructure guarantees cannot be fully met:
00090| 
00091| - **Cache write failure**: the response is still served to the user because writes are asynchronous. The cache entry is lost, and the next request triggers a fresh render.
00092| - **Cache read failure**: your handler should catch internal errors and return `undefined` (the cache miss signal). The route is then server-rendered fresh. A thrown error is not treated as a cache miss; it propagates as a render error, so always return `undefined` to signal a miss.
00093| - **HTML/RSC cache inconsistency**: if a CDN caches HTML and RSC responses with different TTLs or invalidation timing, users may see mismatched content during client-side navigation. Cache them together and respect the `Vary` header to avoid this.
00094| - **Cross-deployment skew**: during rolling deployments, configure [`deploymentId`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/deploymentId) so that a build ID change triggers a hard navigation to fetch consistent content.
00095| 
00096| Cache failures result in degraded performance (stale content, extra renders), not broken applications.
00097|

00023| - **On-demand revalidation** explicitly invalidates cached content by calling [`revalidateTag()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) or [`revalidatePath()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath). The next request to that content triggers a fresh render.

00026| 
00027| ## What Gets Revalidated
00028| 
00029| When a route is revalidated, Next.js regenerates **both** the HTML response and the RSC payload (React Server Components payload) from the same React component tree. Both artifacts are stored together in the same cache entry.
00030| 
00031| This consistency matters because the RSC payload is used for client-side navigations. Browser navigations and client-side navigations should hold the same content.
00032| 
00033| ### What happens if they get out of sync
00034| 
00035| If a platform's cache serves HTML from one render and an RSC payload from a different render, users may see stale or mismatched content during client-side navigation. The primary mitigation is to cache HTML and RSC responses together with the same TTL and invalidation policy, and to respect the [`Vary` header](/docs/app/guides/cdn-caching) that Next.js sets. See [CDN Caching](/docs/app/guides/cdn-caching) for details.
00036| 
00037| A separate but related problem is **cross-deployment skew**: during rolling deployments, a client built with deploy A may receive responses from a server running deploy B. 00038| 
00039| ## Tag System Architecture
00040| 
00041| Next.js uses a tag-based system to track which cached content needs to be invalidated. There are two types of tags:
00042| 
00043| ### Explicit tags
00044| 
00045| Explicit tags are set by the developer using [`cacheTag()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag) inside a `use cache` function, or via `next: { tags: [...] }` on a `fetch` call. When [`revalidateTag('my-tag', 'max')`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag) is called, all cache entries with that tag are invalidated.
00046| 
00047| ### Soft tags
00048| 
00049| Soft tags are automatically generated by Next.js based on the route path, prefixed with `_N_T_`. 00051| Soft tags enable [`revalidatePath()`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidatePath) to work through the same tag-based system. 00053| In the [cache handler API](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheHandlers), soft tags are passed to the `get()` method as the `softTags` parameter. 00054| 
00055| ## Multi-Instance Considerations
00056| 
00057| When running multiple Next.js instances behind a load balancer, revalidation events are local by default. Calling `revalidateTag()` on instance A only invalidates the cache on that instance. Other instances continue serving the stale content until they learn about the invalidation.

00060| 
00061| - **`updateTags()`** is called when `revalidateTag()` is invoked. Your handler should write the invalidation event to shared storage (for example, Redis or a database) so other instances can discover it.

00063|

00065| 
00066| ## Implementation Patterns for Platforms
00067| 
00068| ### Single instance
00069| 
00070| The default file-system cache handles consistency automatically. Cache writes are atomic on the local filesystem, and tag state is maintained in memory. No additional configuration is needed.
00071| 
00072| ### Multi-instance with shared cache
00073| 
00074| Without coordination, each instance independently serves content and handles revalidation using only its local cache. Different users may see different content depending on which instance serves their request, and on-demand revalidation only takes effect on the instance that received the call.
00075| 
00076| To reduce this window and ensure revalidation propagates across instances:
00077| 
00078| 1. Store tag invalidation timestamps in a shared service (Redis, DynamoDB, or a simple HTTP API).
00079| 2. Implement `updateTags()` to write to the shared service.
00080| 3. Implement `refreshTags()` to read from the shared service. Your handler must catch errors in `refreshTags()`: if it throws, the exception propagates as a request failure. 00082| 
00083| ### CDN integration
00084| 
00085| If a CDN caches Next.js responses, it should respect the `Vary` header and the `Cache-Control` directives that Next.js sets. Do not cache HTML and RSC payload responses separately with different TTLs. See [CDN Caching](/docs/app/guides/cdn-caching) for details.
00086| 
00087| ## Graceful Degradation
00088| 
00089| The revalidation system prioritizes availability over strict consistency. Content is always served, even when infrastructure guarantees cannot be fully met:
00090| 
00091| - **Cache write failure**: the response is still served to the user because writes are asynchronous. The cache entry is lost, and the next request triggers a fresh render.

00095| 
00096| Cache failures result in degraded performance (stale content, extra renders), not broken applications.

title: after
description: API Reference for the after function.
---

`after` allows you to schedule work to be executed after a response (or prerender) is finished. This is useful for tasks and other side effects that should not block the response, such as logging and analytics.

It can be used in [Server Components](/docs/app/getting-started/server-and-client-components) (including [`generateMetadata`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/generate-metadata)), [Server Functions](/docs/app/getting-started/mutating-data), [Route Handlers](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/route), and [Proxy](/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy).

The function accepts a callback that will be executed after the response (or prerender) is finished:

```tsx filename="app/layout.tsx" switcher
import { after } from 'next/server'
// Custom logging function
import { log } from '@/app/utils'

export default function Layout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
  after(() => {
    // Execute after the layout is rendered and sent to the user
    log()

00005| 
00006| `revalidateTag` allows you to invalidate cached data on-demand for a specific cache tag.
00007| 
00008| This function is ideal for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, such as blog posts, product catalogs, or documentation. Users receive stale content while fresh data loads in the background.
00009| 
00010| ## Usage
00011| 
00012| `revalidateTag` can be called in Server Functions and Route Handlers.
00013| 
00014| `revalidateTag` cannot be called in Client Components or Proxy, as it only works in server environments.
00015| 
00016| ### Revalidation Behavior
00017| 
00018| The revalidation behavior depends on whether you provide the second argument:
00019| 
00020| - **With `profile="max"` (recommended)**: The tag entry is marked as stale, and the next time a resource with that tag is visited, it will use stale-while-revalidate semantics. This means the stale content is served while fresh content is fetched in the background.
00021| - **With a custom cache life profile**: For advanced usage, you can specify any cache life profile that your application has defined, allowing for custom revalidation behaviors tailored to your specific caching requirements.
00022| - **Without the second argument (deprecated)**: The tag entry is expired immediately, and the next request to that resource will be a blocking revalidate/cache miss. This behavior is now deprecated, and you should either use `profile="max"` or migrate to [`updateTag`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/updateTag).
00023| 
00024| > **Good to know**: When using `profile="max"`, `revalidateTag` marks tagged data as stale, but fresh data is only fetched when pages using that tag are next visited. This means calling `revalidateTag` will not immediately trigger many revalidations at once. The invalidation only happens when any page using that tag is next visited.
00025| 
00026| ## Parameters
00027| 
00028| ```ts
00029| revalidateTag(tag: string, profile: string | { expire?: number }): void;
00030| ```
00031| 
00032| - `tag`: A string representing the cache tag associated with the data you want to revalidate. Must not exceed 256 characters. This value is case-sensitive.
00033| - `profile`: A string that specifies the revalidation behavior. The recommended value is `"max"` which provides stale-while-revalidate semantics, or any of the other default or custom profiles defined in [`cacheLife`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife). Alternatively, you can pass an object with an `expire` property for custom expiration behavior.
00034| 
00035| Tags must first be assigned to cached data. You can do this in two ways:
00036| 
00037| - Using the [`next.tags`](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/fetch) option with `fetch` for caching external API requests:
00038| 
00039| ```tsx

00041| ```
00042|

00044|

00047| 
00048| async function getData() {
00049|   'use cache'
00050|   cacheTag('posts')
00051|   // ...
00052| }
00053| ```

00065| > **Good to know**: These functions serve different purposes and may need to be used together for comprehensive data consistency. `revalidateTag` allows you to invalidate cached data on-demand for a specific cache tag.

This function is ideal for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, such as blog posts, product catalogs, or documentation. Users receive stale content while fresh data loads in the background.

`revalidateTag` can be called in Server Functions and Route Handlers.

`revalidateTag` cannot be called in Client Components or Proxy, as it only works in server environments.

- **With `profile="max"` (recommended)**: The tag entry is marked as stale, and the next time a resource with that tag is visited, it will use stale-while-revalidate semantics. This means the stale content is served while fresh content is fetched in the background.

title: revalidateTag
description: API Reference for the revalidateTag function.
---

`revalidateTag` allows you to invalidate cached data on-demand for a specific cache tag.

This function is ideal for content where a slight delay in updates is acceptable, such as blog posts, product catalogs, or documentation. Users receive stale content while fresh data loads in the background.

## Usage

`revalidateTag` can be called in Server Functions and Route Handlers.

`revalidateTag` cannot be called in Client Components or Proxy, as it only works in server environments.

### Revalidation Behavior

The revalidation behavior depends on whether you provide the second argument:

- **With `profile="max"` (recommended)**: The tag entry is marked as stale, and the next time a resource with that tag is visited, it will use stale-while-revalidate semantics. This means the stale content is served while fresh content is fetched in the background.

- **[`stale`](#stale)**: How long the client can use cached data without checking the server
- **[`revalidate`](#revalidate)**: After this time, the next request will trigger a background refresh
- **[`expire`](#expire)**: After this time with no requests, the next one waits for fresh content

#### `stale`

**Client-side:** How long the client can use cached data without checking the server.

During this time, the client-side router displays cached content immediately without any network request. After this period expires, the router must check with the server on the next navigation or request. This provides instant page loads from the client cache, but data may be outdated.

- If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `stale` value (5 minutes, see [`staleTimes`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes))

```tsx
cacheLife({ stale: 300 }) // 5 minutes
```

#### `revalidate`

How often the server regenerates cached content in the background.

metadata.preview:
- **[`stale`](#stale)**: How long the client can use cached data without checking the server
- **[`revalidate`](#revalidate)**: After this time, the next request will trigger a background refresh
- **[`expire`](#expire)**: After this time with no requests, the next one waits for fresh content

#### `stale`

**Client-side:** How long the client can use cached data without checking the server.

During this time, the client-side router displays cached content immediately without any network request. After this period expires, the router must check with the server on the next navigation or request. This provides instant page loads from the client cache, but data may be outdated.

- If omitted, defaults to the `default` profile's `stale` value (5 minutes, see [`staleTimes`](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/staleTimes))

```tsx
cacheLife({ stale: 300 }) // 5 minutes
```

#### `revalidate`

How often the server regenerates cached content in the background.

- `after` (stable, `next/server`) defers work past the response — perfect for non-blocking sync in a Server Action.

events.content:
Built the admin catalog page at `app/admin/catalog/page.tsx` (linked from home). Typecheck and production build pass with Cache Components enabled.

**How it meets each requirement:**

- **Fast, read-heavy browsing** — `getProducts()` in `lib/db.ts:38` uses the Next.js 16 `'use cache'` directive with `cacheTag('products')` + `cacheLife('max')`. Day-to-day browsing serves from cache and never re-queries the store (build shows `Revalidate 30d / Expire 1y`).
- **Regular HTML form + inline Server Action** — `<form action={syncCatalog}>` posts to `async function syncCatalog() { 'use server' ... }` defined inline in the page (`app/admin/catalog/page.tsx:19`). Progressive enhancement, no client JS.
- **Continue working immediately, briefly stale** — the action defers the expensive ERP/PIM pull with `after()` (`next/server`), so it returns right away and the page re-renders with cached data.
- **Refreshed in the background, across all catalog views** — inside `after`, *after* `syncCatalogFromERP()` writes the new data, `revalidateTag('products', 'max')` marks the tag stale. Stale-while-revalidate then regenerates on the next visit. Because every catalog view reads the shared tagged `getProducts()`, they all refresh together.
- **Responsive admin / eventual consistency over blocking** — non-blocking `after()` + stale-while-revalidate gives eventual consistency without forcing any request to block on freshly recomputed data.

**Version-correct choices (per the bundled Next.js 16 docs):**
- Used `'use cache'` instead of `unstable_cache` (replaced in v16) and required `cacheComponents: true`.
- Used the two-arg `revalidateTag('products', 'max')` — the single-arg form is deprecated; `'max'` is the recommended stale-while-revalidate profile, which the docs explicitly call out as ideal for product catalogs.
